raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old pre-morbid healthy male patient was referred to our hospital with complaints of giddiness and loss of balance while walking since 1 month associated with mild, throbbing, generalized headache. There was no history of nausea, vomiting, seizure, syncope, preceding head injury or any addictions. About 1 month back, patient was admitted to a local hospital with complaints of fever with chills, for which patient was treated with Ceftriaxone and Amikacin for 3 days. No history of patient having received anti-malarial in any form. Patient's fever did subside but then he developed giddiness and started requiring support for walking. Patient received symptomatic treatment but had no symptom relief hence a CT scan of head was done, which was apparently normal. There was no drug-history suggestive of cause for his ataxia. Due to persistence of symptoms the patient was referred to our center for further management. On admission to our hospital, his pulse was 72/min, blood pressure 100/70 mm of Hg, respiratory rate 18 cycles/min, afebrile, pallor was present; no icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, edema; jugular venous pressure was normal. There was no evidence of any neurocutaneous markers. Cardiovascular and respiratory systems' examination were unremarkable. Per abdomen examination was suggestive of splenomegaly (palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin), no hepatomegaly. On neurological examination, he was fully alert, conscious and oriented to time, place and person. On higher mental examination only attention span was reduced. All cranial nerves and sensory system were normal. On motor system examination, he had hypotonia in all limbs. All superficial reflexes were normal with bilateral plantars flexors. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in upper limbs and exaggerated in lower limbs with pendular knee jerks in both the lower limbs. Finger-Nose Test, Knee-Heel test, Dysdiadokokinesis, Tandem Gait were bilaterally impaired. Nystagmus-Absent. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. His laboratory investigations were as follows: Hb-9.9 G%, WBC-5800 cumm of blood, Polymorphs-70% Lymphocytes-26%, Monocytes-1%, Eosinophils-3%, Platelet Count-1.8 lakh. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm at the end of 1 h.
Peripheral smear showed gametes and rings of plasmodium falciparum malaria with parasitic index-2.8%. Random blood sugar-83 mg/dl, blood urea-22 mg/dl, serum creatinine-1.2 mg/dl, serum sodium-136 mEq/L, serum potassium-3.8 mEq/L.
MRI Brain-Normal study.
Cerebrospinal Fluid Analysis-Normal study.
Serum Vitamin B12 levels-Within normal limits.
Serum Thiamine levels-Within normal limits.
Chest X-Ray PA View-Within normal limits.
ECG 12 Leads-Within normal limits.
USG (Abdomen + Pelvis)-Splenomegaly (16 cms).
He was started on quinine sulphate orally, along with pyrimethamine and sulfadoxine on doses recommended by WHO 2010 guidelines for treatment of malaria. His cerebellar signs showed a complete recovery in 14 days with waxing and waning phenomenon. He did not require any steroids. He was discharged after 14 days in a hemodynamically stable condition and with no neurodeficit.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male presenting with progressive giddiness, severe gait ataxia, and mild throbbing headache persisting for 1 month following a febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to referral, the patient was hospitalized with acute fever and chills and treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and amikacin for 3 days without antimalarials. Although his fever subsided, he developed severe imbalance, dizziness, and cerebellar ataxia requiring support to ambulate. An initial non-contrast head CT was normal. Due to persistent gait impairment and generalized throbbing headache, he was referred to a tertiary neurology center.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Hospitalized 1 month prior with fever and chills, treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and amikacin for 3 days; no antimalarials administered. Denied history of head trauma, seizures, syncope, or substance abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dizziness, gait unsteadiness, mild headache, and reduced attention span. Negative for nausea, vomiting, seizures, syncope, visual changes, or sensory loss. Medications: symptomatic agents without relief. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Pulse rate: 72 beats/min, blood pressure: 100/70 mmHg, respiratory rate: 18 cycles/min, afebrile. Marked pallor present; no icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or peripheral edema; jugular venous pressure normal. Abdomen: Splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin; no hepatomegaly. Neurological: Alert, conscious, oriented; attention span reduced. Cranial nerves and sensory system normal. Motor: Hypotonia in all limbs; upper limb deep tendon reflexes normal, lower limb reflexes exaggerated with bilateral pendular knee jerks; bilateral plantar responses flexor. Cerebellar signs: Bilateral impairment on finger-to-nose testing, heel-to-knee testing, dysdiadochokinesia, and tandem gait; nystagmus absent. Meningeal signs absent.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 9.9 g%, white blood cell count: 5,800/cumm (polymorphs: 70%, lymphocytes: 26%, monocytes: 1%, eosinophils: 3%), platelet count: 1.8 lakh (180,000/mm3). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 110 mm at the end of 1 hour. Random blood sugar: 83 mg/dL, blood urea: 22 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL, serum sodium: 136 mEq/L, serum potassium: 3.8 mEq/L. Serum vitamin B12: Within normal limits. Serum thiamine: Within normal limits. Chest X-ray (PA view): Within normal limits. 12-lead ECG: Within normal limits. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound: Splenomegaly (spleen span 16 cm).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: Normal study. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Normal cytochemical study. Prior head CT: Apparently normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Delayed cerebellar ataxia (post-malaria neurological syndrome / acute cerebellar ataxia) associated with persistent Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia and splenomegaly.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated gametes and ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitic index of 2.8%. Structural intracranial pathology, thiamine/B12 deficiency, and CNS infection were excluded by normal brain MRI, normal CSF analysis, and normal vitamin levels.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral quinine sulphate along with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine according to WHO 2010 guidelines. Cerebellar ataxia demonstrated complete recovery over 14 days with a characteristic waxing and waning pattern, without requiring corticosteroids. Discharged home after 14 days hemodynamically stable with complete resolution of neurological deficits.
